warmup.q: A Kotlin service exposes payment events as a MutableStateFlow<Posted>. A card buys two 4.50 coffees, so Posted("acc-1", 450) is set twice in a row. How many of those does a collector see?
warmup.why: StateFlow conflates values with equals: setting a value equal to the current one does nothing, so the second coffee never reaches collectors. That is right for state (the latest balance) and wrong for events. A MutableSharedFlow delivers both.

sections.h: Observer: tell the listeners, then stay out of their way
sections.html:
A posting hits the ledger, and four parts of the service care: the balance view, the receipt email, analytics and fraud scoring. If post calls all four directly, the ledger depends on every one of them, and a broken analytics endpoint makes postings fail. Observer inverts that. The ledger, the subject, keeps a list of listeners and tells each one what happened. It doesn't know who they are.

Java
final class EventBus<E> {
    private final List<Consumer<? super E>> listeners = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>();

    AutoCloseable subscribe(Consumer<? super E> listener) {
        listeners.add(listener);
        return () -> listeners.remove(listener);          // the handle that prevents leaks
    }

    void publish(E event) {
        for (Consumer<? super E> l : listeners) {
            try {
                l.accept(event);
            } catch (RuntimeException e) {
                log.warn("listener failed", e);           // one bad listener must not starve the rest
            }
        }
    }
}
Kotlin
class EventBus<E> {
    private val listeners = CopyOnWriteArrayList<(E) -> Unit>()

    fun subscribe(listener: (E) -> Unit): AutoCloseable {
        listeners += listener
        return AutoCloseable { listeners -= listener }    // the handle that prevents leaks
    }

    fun publish(event: E) {
        for (l in listeners) {
            try {
                l(event)
            } catch (e: RuntimeException) {
                log.warn("listener failed", e)            // one bad listener must not starve the rest
            }
        }
    }
}

No PaymentListener interface: Consumer<E> in Java and (E) -> Unit in Kotlin already say "something that takes an event".

Each line here prevents a real bug. subscribe returns a handle, because a listener that is never removed is a lapsed listener: the bus holds a reference to it forever, so it can't be garbage collected and keeps reacting to events long after its owner is gone. The try/catch stops one failing listener from cancelling delivery to the ones after it. CopyOnWriteArrayList iterates over a snapshot, so a listener may unsubscribe while it is being called; with an ArrayList, that throws ConcurrentModificationException. Copy-on-write makes every subscribe expensive and every publish cheap, which fits listener lists.

One property stays, whatever you do: delivery is synchronous. Every listener runs on the publishing thread, inside post. A 300 ms email call makes every posting 300 ms slower, and a listener that publishes another event starts a nested round of delivery before the first round is done. Keep in-process listeners fast, and hand slow work to a queue.

try.title: Break a listener, then remove the safety net
steps: Read EventBusDemo.java (or EventBusDemo.kt). Three listeners subscribe; the second always throws. Predict the five lines it prints.
Run it with the command below.
Delete the try/catch in publish, keeping the l.accept(event) (l(event) in Kotlin) line. Predict, then run. Put it back.

code.title: EventBusDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l08; import java.util.List; import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList; import java.util.function.Consumer; /** A hand-rolled Observer: subscribe returns a handle, and one bad listener can't starve the rest. */ public class EventBusDemo { static final class EventBus<E> { private final List<Consumer<? super E>> listeners = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); AutoCloseable subscribe(Consumer<? super E> listener) { listeners.add(listener); return () -> listeners.remove(listener); // the handle that prevents leaks } void publish(E event) { for (Consumer<? super E> l : listeners) { try { l.accept(event); } catch (RuntimeException e) { // isolate each listener System.out.println(" (a listener failed: " + e.getMessage() + ")"); } } } } record Posted(String account, long amountMinor) {} public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { EventBus<Posted> bus = new EventBus<>(); bus.subscribe(e -> System.out.println("ledger view got " + e)); bus.subscribe(e -> { throw new IllegalStateException("analytics dashboard is down"); }); AutoCloseable email = bus.subscribe(e -> System.out.println("email sender got " + e)); bus.publish(new Posted("acc-1", 450)); email.close(); // unsubscribe bus.publish(new Posted("acc-1", 900)); } }

alt.title: EventBusDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l08 import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList // A hand-rolled Observer: subscribe returns a handle, and one bad listener can't starve the rest. class EventBus<E> { private val listeners = CopyOnWriteArrayList<(E) -> Unit>() fun subscribe(listener: (E) -> Unit): AutoCloseable { listeners += listener return AutoCloseable { listeners -= listener } // the handle that prevents leaks } fun publish(event: E) { for (l in listeners) { try { l(event) } catch (e: RuntimeException) { // isolate each listener println(" (a listener failed: ${e.message})") } } } } data class PostedEvent(val account: String, val amountMinor: Long) fun main() { val bus = EventBus<PostedEvent>() bus.subscribe { println("ledger view got $it") } bus.subscribe { throw IllegalStateException("analytics dashboard is down") } val email = bus.subscribe { println("email sender got $it") } bus.publish(PostedEvent("acc-1", 450)) email.close() // unsubscribe bus.publish(PostedEvent("acc-1", 900)) }

try.expect: The ledger view and the email sender both get the 450 posting, with (a listener failed: analytics dashboard is down) between them. After email.close(), only the ledger view gets the 900 posting. Without the try/catch, the program prints the first ledger line and dies with IllegalStateException: analytics dashboard is down: the email sender never hears anything, and in a service the posting itself would fail.

sections.h: Flows are observers with the bookkeeping done
sections.html:
Kotlin's coroutine library ships two ready-made subjects. A SharedFlow broadcasts every emitted value to every active collector. A StateFlow holds one current value: "a state flow is a hot flow", it "never completes", and each collector gets the current value first, then every change. Both are thread-safe, and both do the bookkeeping from the last section for you. There is no listener list to guard. Cancelling the collecting coroutine unsubscribes it, and each collector runs in its own coroutine, so one that fails doesn't stop the others.

Java
// Closest Java equivalent: the JDK's java.util.concurrent.Flow, with SubmissionPublisher as a hot publisher
SubmissionPublisher<String> events = new SubmissionPublisher<>();
CompletableFuture<Void> done = events.consume(e -> System.out.println("got " + e));   // one subscriber
events.submit("AUTHORIZED");
events.submit("AUTHORIZED");          // delivered again: a publisher has no idea of "same as last time"
events.close();                       // completes the stream; done completes after the last item
Kotlin
class PaymentStatus {
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow("NEW")
    val state: StateFlow<String> = _state.asStateFlow()          // state: the latest value

    private val _events = MutableSharedFlow<String>()
    val events: SharedFlow<String> = _events.asSharedFlow()     // events: every one, to every collector

    suspend fun on(event: String) {
        _events.emit(event)       // with no buffer, waits until every current collector has taken it
        _state.value = event
    }
}

Keep the mutable flow private and expose the read-only type, as above. Use _state.update { ... } when the new value depends on the old one, because it is an atomic read-modify-write.

The rule that matters for payments is in the StateFlow docs: values "are conflated using Any.equals comparison in a similar way to distinctUntilChanged", and "a slow collector skips fast updates". That is exactly right for state. A dashboard showing a payment's status needs only the latest one. It is wrong for events. Two 4.50 coffees on the same card, Posted("acc-1", 450) twice, arrive as one, and a slow consumer misses the updates in between. Use a SharedFlow for events, or a Channel when each item must go to exactly one consumer.

Java has the interfaces but few implementations. java.util.concurrent.Flow holds the Reactive Streams types (Publisher, Subscriber, Subscription), and SubmissionPublisher is the one hot publisher in the JDK. In Reactor, a Flux is the same idea with backpressure, and Sinks.many().multicast() plays the role of a MutableSharedFlow. None of them drops equal values unless you ask with distinctUntilChanged().

try.title: Watch StateFlow drop an event
steps: Read StateVsShared.kt (or the Java twin, StateVsSharedJava.java). The same three updates go to a state holder and an event stream. Predict both lines.
Run it with the command below.
Kotlin: change val events = MutableSharedFlow<String>() to val events = MutableStateFlow("NEW") and run. Java: delete the if (Objects.equals(value, next)) return; line and run. Predict each first.

code.title: StateVsShared.kt
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l08 import kotlinx.coroutines.CoroutineStart import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.MutableSharedFlow import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.MutableStateFlow import kotlinx.coroutines.launch import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking import kotlinx.coroutines.yield // The same three payment updates, observed through a StateFlow and through a SharedFlow. fun main() = runBlocking { val state = MutableStateFlow("NEW") // state: the latest value; equal values are dropped val events = MutableSharedFlow<String>() // events: every value, to every collector val fromState = mutableListOf<String>() val fromEvents = mutableListOf<String>() val collectors = listOf( launch(start = CoroutineStart.UNDISPATCHED) { state.collect { fromState += it } }, launch(start = CoroutineStart.UNDISPATCHED) { events.collect { fromEvents += it } }, ) for (update in listOf("AUTHORIZED", "AUTHORIZED", "CAPTURED")) { state.value = update events.emit(update) // suspends until every collector has taken it yield() } collectors.forEach { it.cancel() } println("StateFlow collector saw: $fromState") println("SharedFlow collector saw: $fromEvents") }

alt.title: StateVsSharedJava.java
alt.html: // Closest Java equivalent: the JDK's Flow API, where SubmissionPublisher delivers every event, plus a tiny // "latest value" holder that drops equal values the way Kotlin's StateFlow does. The JDK has no StateFlow. package workbench.patterns.l08; import java.util.List; import java.util.Objects; import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture; import java.util.concurrent.CopyOnWriteArrayList; import java.util.concurrent.SubmissionPublisher; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.function.Consumer; public class StateVsSharedJava { /** Holds one current value and tells observers about changes; equal values are dropped. */ static final class LatestValue<T> { private final List<Consumer<T>> observers = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); private T value; LatestValue(T initial) { value = initial; } synchronized void set(T next) { if (Objects.equals(value, next)) return; // StateFlow-style conflation by equals() value = next; observers.forEach(o -> o.accept(next)); } synchronized void observe(Consumer<T> o) { observers.add(o); o.accept(value); // new observers get the current value first } } public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { LatestValue<String> state = new LatestValue<>("NEW"); List<String> fromState = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); state.observe(fromState::add); List<String> fromEvents = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); CompletableFuture<Void> done; try (SubmissionPublisher<String> events = new SubmissionPublisher<>()) { done = events.consume(fromEvents::add); // a subscriber that gets every item for (String update : List.of("AUTHORIZED", "AUTHORIZED", "CAPTURED")) { state.set(update); events.submit(update); } } // close() completes the stream done.get(5, TimeUnit.SECONDS); System.out.println("state holder saw: " + fromState); System.out.println("event publisher saw: " + fromEvents); } }

try.expect: The state side prints [NEW, AUTHORIZED, CAPTURED]: the initial value, then only real changes. The event side prints [AUTHORIZED, AUTHORIZED, CAPTURED]: every event. With a StateFlow for events, the Kotlin event line becomes [NEW, AUTHORIZED, CAPTURED], so the second authorization is gone and a fake NEW event appeared. Without the equality check, the Java state holder prints [NEW, AUTHORIZED, AUTHORIZED, CAPTURED]: that one check is the whole difference.

sections.h: Command: a request you can store, queue and undo
sections.html:
Command turns a request into an object: what to do and with which arguments, as a value you can keep. Once a request is a value, you can queue it, log it, retry it and undo it.

For a ledger, a sealed interface of records is the natural shape:

Java
sealed interface Command permits Deposit, Withdraw {
    void apply(Account a);
    void undo(Account a);
}
record Deposit(long amount) implements Command {
    public void apply(Account a) { a.balance += amount; }
    public void undo(Account a)  { a.balance -= amount; }
}
record Withdraw(long amount) implements Command {
    public void apply(Account a) {
        if (a.balance < amount) throw new IllegalStateException("insufficient funds");
        a.balance -= amount;
    }
    public void undo(Account a)  { a.balance += amount; }
}

final class CommandLog {
    private final Deque<Command> history = new ArrayDeque<>();
    void run(Command c, Account a) { c.apply(a); history.push(c); }    // record only after success
    void undoLast(Account a) { Command c = history.poll(); if (c != null) c.undo(a); }
}
Kotlin
sealed interface Command {
    fun apply(a: Account)
    fun undo(a: Account)
}
data class Deposit(val amount: Long) : Command {
    override fun apply(a: Account) { a.balance += amount }
    override fun undo(a: Account) { a.balance -= amount }
}
data class Withdraw(val amount: Long) : Command {
    override fun apply(a: Account) {
        check(a.balance >= amount) { "insufficient funds" }
        a.balance -= amount
    }
    override fun undo(a: Account) { a.balance += amount }
}

class CommandLog {
    private val history = ArrayDeque<Command>()
    fun run(c: Command, a: Account) { c.apply(a); history.addFirst(c) }   // record only after success
    fun undoLast(a: Account) { history.removeFirstOrNull()?.undo(a) }
}

Two details carry the pattern. First, run records the command only after apply succeeds. Record it first, and a rejected 1,000.00 withdrawal sits in the history, so the next undo "refunds" money that never left. Second, the commands are data. Withdraw(amount=30) prints well, compares by value, and can be serialized and written to a table.

When a command needs no undo and no data, the class disappears. Runnable, Callable and () -> Unit are commands, and executor.submit(() -> settle(batchId)) hands one to a queue that a worker drains. Keep a named class when you need what a lambda can't give: equality, a readable log line, serialization, or a second method such as undo.

try.title: Record the command too early
steps: Run UndoDemo in either language and read the three lines.
In CommandLog.run, swap the two lines so the command is recorded before it is applied. Predict the history and the balance after one undo, then run.

code.title: UndoDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.patterns.l08; import java.util.ArrayDeque; import java.util.Deque; /** Commands as records, an undo log, and the one rule that keeps undo honest. */ public class UndoDemo { static final class Wallet { long balance; } sealed interface Command permits Deposit, Withdraw { void apply(Wallet w); void undo(Wallet w); } record Deposit(long amount) implements Command { public void apply(Wallet w) { w.balance += amount; } public void undo(Wallet w) { w.balance -= amount; } } record Withdraw(long amount) implements Command { public void apply(Wallet w) { if (w.balance < amount) throw new IllegalStateException("insufficient funds"); w.balance -= amount; } public void undo(Wallet w) { w.balance += amount; } } static final class CommandLog { final Deque<Command> history = new ArrayDeque<>(); void run(Command c, Wallet w) { c.apply(w); // 1. apply first history.push(c); // 2. record only after it worked } void undoLast(Wallet w) { Command c = history.poll(); if (c != null) c.undo(w); } } public static void main(String[] args) { Wallet wallet = new Wallet(); CommandLog log = new CommandLog(); log.run(new Deposit(100), wallet); log.run(new Withdraw(30), wallet); try { log.run(new Withdraw(1_000), wallet); } catch (IllegalStateException e) { System.out.println("rejected: " + e.getMessage()); } System.out.println("balance " + wallet.balance + ", history " + log.history); log.undoLast(wallet); System.out.println("after one undo: balance " + wallet.balance + ", history " + log.history); } }

alt.title: UndoDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.patterns.l08 // Commands as data classes, an undo log, and the one rule that keeps undo honest. class Wallet { var balance = 0L } sealed interface WalletCommand { fun apply(w: Wallet) fun undo(w: Wallet) data class Deposit(val amount: Long) : WalletCommand { override fun apply(w: Wallet) { w.balance += amount } override fun undo(w: Wallet) { w.balance -= amount } } data class Withdraw(val amount: Long) : WalletCommand { override fun apply(w: Wallet) { check(w.balance >= amount) { "insufficient funds" } w.balance -= amount } override fun undo(w: Wallet) { w.balance += amount } } } class CommandLog { val history = ArrayDeque<WalletCommand>() fun run(c: WalletCommand, w: Wallet) { c.apply(w) // 1. apply first history.addFirst(c) // 2. record only after it worked } fun undoLast(w: Wallet) { history.removeFirstOrNull()?.undo(w) } } fun main() { val wallet = Wallet() val log = CommandLog() log.run(WalletCommand.Deposit(100), wallet) log.run(WalletCommand.Withdraw(30), wallet) try { log.run(WalletCommand.Withdraw(1_000), wallet) } catch (e: IllegalStateException) { println("rejected: ${e.message}") } println("balance ${wallet.balance}, history ${log.history}") log.undoLast(wallet) println("after one undo: balance ${wallet.balance}, history ${log.history}") }

try.expect: rejected: insufficient funds, then balance 70 with a history of Withdraw 30 and Deposit 100, then after one undo: balance 100. With the lines swapped, the rejected Withdraw of 1,000 sits on top of the history, and the undo puts 1,000 back that never left: balance 1070.

sections.html:
Once a command is a record, it can leave the process, and most commands in a payment system do.

The transactional outbox is a queue of commands that survives crashes. In the same database transaction that captures a payment, you insert a row saying "send receipt for payment 7781". A relay reads new rows and publishes them to Kafka, and a consumer executes them. Either both the capture and the command commit, or neither does, so a crash between the two can't lose the receipt.

Temporal is built on the same idea. When a workflow calls a method on an activity stub, the SDK doesn't run your activity there. It records a command to schedule that activity, with its name and arguments, in the workflow's history, and a worker picks it up. If the worker dies, Temporal schedules it again, according to the retry options.

Both deliver at least once. A stored command can run twice: the relay crashed after publishing but before marking the row sent, or the activity finished but its result was lost. So every command that leaves the process must be idempotent. Charge with an idempotency key, and make "send receipt 7781" a no-op the second time.

Undo changes meaning too. In memory, undo puts the old state back. Across systems you can't un-send money. A captured payment is reversed by a new command, a Refund, with its own record, its own fees and its own failure modes. Sagas, including Temporal's, are lists of such compensating commands, run in reverse when a later step fails. Model a refund as a compensation, never as undo of a charge.

Check yourself. The outbox relay publishes "send receipt for payment 7781" to Kafka, then crashes before it marks the row sent. It restarts. How many receipts does the customer get if the consumer just sends one per message, and what fixes it? (Two, because the relay publishes the row again. The consumer must remember which payment ids it has already sent a receipt for, and skip a repeat.)

It is either run now, applied and pushed on an undo stack, or stored in an outbox row, Kafka or Temporal history and run later by a worker, possibly twice"><rect class="box" x="16" y="96" width="104" height="52" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="68" y="118" text-anchor="middle">caller</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="68" y="137" text-anchor="middle">API, consumer</text><rect class="box-a" x="160" y="88" width="180" height="68" rx="8"/><text class="t t-code" x="250" y="116" text-anchor="middle">Capture(id, 1250)</text><text class="t-s" x="250" y="138" text-anchor="middle">a command is data</text><rect class="box" x="384" y="22" width="280" height="60" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="524" y="46" text-anchor="middle">run now</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="524" y="66" text-anchor="middle">apply, then push on the undo stack</text><rect class="box-b" x="384" y="160" width="280" height="60" rx="8"/><text class="t" x="524" y="184" text-anchor="middle">store, run later</text><text class="t-s t-m" x="524" y="204" text-anchor="middle">outbox row, Kafka, Temporal history</text><line class="ln-a" x1="120" y1="122" x2="156" y2="122" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><line class="ln" x1="340" y1="108" x2="380" y2="58" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><line class="ln" x1="340" y1="138" x2="380" y2="186" marker-end="url(#arr)"/><text class="t-s t-bad" x="524" y="240" text-anchor="middle">a stored command can run twice: make it idempotent</text></svg>
figure.caption: A command is data. Run now, it goes on an undo stack; stored, it goes through an outbox, Kafka or Temporal, and may run more than once.

analogy: Observer is a newsletter: the publisher sends each issue to whoever is on the list, and every issue carries an unsubscribe link, which is the handle subscribe returns. Command is a restaurant order ticket. The waiter writes the order down instead of cooking it, puts it on the rail, and a cook works through the rail in order. A ticket can be voided before it's cooked, which is undo. Once the meal is served you can't un-serve it, so you comp a dessert, which is compensation. The analogy breaks on duplicates. A kitchen never cooks the same ticket twice by accident, but a message queue or a Temporal retry can deliver the same command twice, so the command itself must be safe to run again.
world: A Kafka consumer group is a durable observer of a topic: it keeps its position in the log, so it can catch up after a crash, which no in-process listener can. Quarkus has the in-process kind built in through CDI events: Event<PaymentCaptured>.fire() on one side and an @Observes method on the other. Use those for fast, losable work, such as metrics and cache eviction. Anything that must not be lost, like a receipt, a ledger entry or fraud scoring, goes through an outbox row and Kafka. On the command side, every Temporal activity call is a command recorded in the workflow history and retried by policy, and your capture, refund and payout activities should all take an idempotency key.
mistake: The most common mistake is using a StateFlow (or a "latest value" holder) for events. It looks like the obvious hot flow: it's thread-safe, it has a value, and the docs example is a counter. Then two identical postings, two equal status updates or two equal webhook notifications arrive in a row, and collectors see one. A slow collector also skips intermediate values, which for a payment can mean never seeing AUTHORIZED between NEW and CAPTURED. The rule: state goes in a StateFlow (only the latest value matters), events go in a SharedFlow or a Channel (each one matters). If a test emits two equal events and expects two, you'll catch it before production does.

compare.title: A command queue drained by one worker

java.title: LedgerWorker.java
java.html: sealed interface LedgerCommand permits Deposit, Withdraw, Stop {} record Deposit(String account, long amountMinor) implements LedgerCommand {} record Withdraw(String account, long amountMinor) implements LedgerCommand {} record Stop() implements LedgerCommand {} // poison pill: a Java queue can't be closed final class LedgerWorker implements Runnable { private final BlockingQueue<LedgerCommand> queue = new ArrayBlockingQueue<>(1_000); // bounded: put blocks when full private final Map<String, Long> balances = new HashMap<>(); // touched only by the thread running run() void submit(LedgerCommand c) throws InterruptedException { queue.put(c); } void stop() throws InterruptedException { queue.put(new Stop()); } @Override public void run() { try { while (true) { switch (queue.take()) { // commands are data: switch on them case Deposit d -> balances.merge(d.account(), d.amountMinor(), Long::sum); case Withdraw w -> balances.merge(w.account(), -w.amountMinor(), Long::sum); case Stop s -> { return; } } } } catch (InterruptedException e) { Thread.currentThread().interrupt(); } } } // start it after construction, never from the constructor: // Thread.ofVirtual().start(worker);

kotlin.title: LedgerWorker.kt
kotlin.html: sealed interface LedgerCommand { data class Deposit(val account: String, val amountMinor: Long) : LedgerCommand data class Withdraw(val account: String, val amountMinor: Long) : LedgerCommand } class LedgerWorker { private val queue = Channel<LedgerCommand>(capacity = 1_000) // bounded: send suspends when full private val balances = mutableMapOf<String, Long>() // touched only by the coroutine in start() fun start(scope: CoroutineScope): Job = scope.launch { for (c in queue) { // ends after stop(), once the queue is drained when (c) { // commands are data: when on them is LedgerCommand.Deposit -> balances.merge(c.account, c.amountMinor) { a, b -> a + b } is LedgerCommand.Withdraw -> balances.merge(c.account, -c.amountMinor) { a, b -> a + b } } } } suspend fun submit(c: LedgerCommand) = queue.send(c) fun stop() = queue.close() // a closed channel is the poison pill }

compare.note: The shape is the same: commands are sealed data, a bounded queue holds them, and one worker applies them in order, so the balances map needs no lock because only one thread or coroutine ever touches it. Two things differ. A Kotlin Channel can be closed, and for (c in queue) ends after the last queued command, so the Stop poison-pill command that Java needs disappears. And send suspends the coroutine when the queue is full, where Java's put blocks a thread; with virtual threads that blocking is cheap too, so the real gain is the built-in close. Neither language needs a Command class hierarchy with an execute() method: a sealed type plus an exhaustive switch or when in the worker does that job.

worked.title: Take side effects out of the ledger's post method

steps.say: The ledger's post grew one call at a time. Before reading on, list what happens to a posting when the analytics service is down.
steps.code: void post(Posting p) { repository.insert(p); balances.add(p.account(), p.amountMinor()); receipts.send(p); // 300 ms SMTP call analytics.track(p); // throws when the dashboard is down fraud.score(p); }

alt.html: fun post(p: Posting) { repository.insert(p) balances.add(p.account, p.amountMinor) receipts.send(p) // 300 ms SMTP call analytics.track(p) // throws when the dashboard is down fraud.score(p) }

steps.say: The posting is already stored, but post throws, so the caller retries and may post twice. Fraud scoring is skipped, and every posting waits for SMTP. First split by what the work needs: the insert and the balance are the posting itself; the rest are reactions to it.
steps.code: void post(Posting p) { repository.insert(p); // 1. the posting itself balances.add(p.account(), p.amountMinor()); bus.publish(new Posted(p.account(), p.amountMinor())); // 2. everything else is a reaction }

alt.html: fun post(p: Posting) { repository.insert(p) // 1. the posting itself balances.add(p.account, p.amountMinor) bus.publish(Posted(p.account, p.amountMinor)) // 2. everything else is a reaction }

steps.say: Wire the reactions in one place at startup. The bus isolates failures, so a broken dashboard costs one log line. Which of these listeners can we afford to lose if the pod dies right after the insert?
steps.code: bus.subscribe(e -> metrics.increment("ledger.posted")); // 3. fast and losable: fine in-process bus.subscribe(e -> analytics.track(e)); // a missed event is a dashboard blip // receipts and fraud scoring are NOT subscribed here: see the next step

alt.html: bus.subscribe { metrics.increment("ledger.posted") } // 3. fast and losable: fine in-process bus.subscribe { analytics.track(it) } // a missed event is a dashboard blip // receipts and fraud scoring are NOT subscribed here: see the next step

steps.say: Receipts and fraud scoring must survive a crash, so they become stored commands: outbox rows written in the same transaction as the posting. A relay publishes them to Kafka, and each consumer handles a command at least once, so it must be idempotent.
steps.code: @Transactional void post(Posting p) { repository.insert(p); balances.add(p.account(), p.amountMinor()); outbox.insert(new OutboxRow("receipt.send", p.id())); // 4. same transaction: both commit or neither outbox.insert(new OutboxRow("fraud.score", p.id())); bus.publish(new Posted(p.account(), p.amountMinor())); // 5. in-process listeners: best effort only }

alt.html: @Transactional fun post(p: Posting) { repository.insert(p) balances.add(p.account, p.amountMinor) outbox.insert(OutboxRow("receipt.send", p.id)) // 4. same transaction: both commit or neither outbox.insert(OutboxRow("fraud.score", p.id)) bus.publish(Posted(p.account, p.amountMinor)) // 5. in-process listeners: best effort only }

lab.title: An observable ledger and an undoable command stack
steps: Run the tests once: all eight fail.

In ObservableLedger, add a private MutableSharedFlow<Posted> and a private MutableStateFlow(0L), and replace the two get() = TODO(...) getters with read-only views of them (= _events.asSharedFlow(), = _balance.asStateFlow()).
Write subscribe with a list that tolerates removal during iteration, returning an AutoCloseable that removes the listener.
Write post: update the balance atomically, call each listener inside its own try/catch, then emit the event.
In CommandStack.kt, write apply and undo for Deposit and Withdraw, then run, undo and redo with two ArrayDeques.
Run the tests until all eight pass.
hints: CopyOnWriteArrayList<(Posted) -> Unit>() gives you snapshot iteration. AutoCloseable { listeners -= listener } is the handle.
_balance.update { it + amountMinor } is an atomic read-modify-write. A MutableSharedFlow with no replay delivers only to collectors that are already collecting, which is what the test sets up.
In run, call cmd.apply(account) before you touch either deque: if it throws, nothing else runs. removeFirstOrNull() ?: return false handles the empty cases in undo and redo.

drill.title: An event bus from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write a generic EventBus<E> with subscribe and publish. It must survive a listener that unsubscribes itself during delivery and a listener that throws, and it must give every subscriber a way to leave. Then compare: which of the three did you miss?

answer.html: final class EventBus<E> { private final List<Consumer<? super E>> listeners = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); // snapshot iteration AutoCloseable subscribe(Consumer<? super E> listener) { listeners.add(listener); return () -> listeners.remove(listener); // the way to leave } void publish(E event) { for (Consumer<? super E> l : listeners) { try { l.accept(event); } catch (RuntimeException e) { // log it; the next listener still runs } } } }

alt.title: Kotlin
alt.html: class EventBus<E> { private val listeners = CopyOnWriteArrayList<(E) -> Unit>() // snapshot iteration fun subscribe(listener: (E) -> Unit): AutoCloseable { listeners += listener return AutoCloseable { listeners -= listener } // the way to leave } fun publish(event: E) { for (l in listeners) { try { l(event) } catch (e: RuntimeException) { // log it; the next listener still runs } } } }

recap: Observer: the subject keeps a list of listeners and tells each one what happened, without knowing who they are. Consumer<E> and (E) -> Unit replace listener interfaces.
A safe listener list returns an unsubscribe handle, isolates each listener's failures, and iterates a snapshot (CopyOnWriteArrayList). Delivery is still synchronous, so keep listeners fast.
Use a StateFlow for state and a SharedFlow (or Channel) for events: StateFlow drops values equal to the current one, and slow collectors skip updates.
Command turns a request into a value you can queue, log, retry and undo. Sealed records or data classes are the natural shape; Runnable and () -> Unit are commands without data.
Record a command for undo only after it succeeded.
Stored commands (outbox rows, Kafka messages, Temporal activities) can run twice, so make them idempotent, and reverse money with a compensating command such as Refund.

explain.prompt: Explain to a teammate why the ledger's balance is a StateFlow but its events are a SharedFlow, using two 4.50 coffee purchases on the same card as your example.
explain.answer: The balance is state: whoever looks at it only needs the latest number. If it goes from 0 to 450 to 900 faster than a dashboard redraws, showing 900 is correct, and if a posting left it unchanged there's nothing new to tell anyone. StateFlow does exactly that: it keeps the current value, gives it to new collectors right away, and drops repeats and intermediate values. The events are different, because each one is a fact someone must act on. Two coffees produce two equal Posted("acc-1", 450) events. A StateFlow would treat the second as "no change" and drop it, so the receipt service would send one receipt and fraud scoring would see one purchase. A SharedFlow delivers every emitted value to every collector, so both coffees arrive.

deeper.html:
StateFlow is a special case of SharedFlow. Its docs describe it as a MutableSharedFlow(replay = 1, onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.DROP_OLDEST) combined with distinctUntilChanged(). Knowing the knobs helps when neither default fits. replay sets how many past values a new collector gets. extraBufferCapacity lets emit run ahead of slow collectors without suspending. onBufferOverflow decides what happens when that buffer is full: suspend the emitter, drop the oldest value or drop the newest. For payment events, the default (suspend) is the safe choice, because dropping is silent.

Kotlin also has an observer for a single property: var status by Delegates.observable("NEW") { _, old, new -> log("$old -> $new") } calls the handler after every assignment, and Delegates.vetoable runs before the assignment and can reject it. They are handy for in-object state, and they are synchronous, like a hand-rolled listener list.

Java has a history here. java.util.Observable and java.util.Observer shipped in Java 1.0 and were deprecated in Java 9. Observable is a class you must extend, its notification order is unspecified, and it isn't a good fit for concurrent code. Use a Consumer list, SubmissionPublisher or a reactive library instead.

Undo for operations that can't be inverted, such as "apply discount rules" or "reformat the draft", doesn't fit the apply/undo pair. There, save a snapshot of the state before the command and restore it on undo. That is the Memento pattern, in lesson 10 of this track, Visitor, Iterator, Mediator and Memento.
